name: Caroli disease
aliases: communicating cavernous ectasia of bile ducts

reference.source: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System / Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Characterised by congenital saccular or fusiform dilatation of the intrahepatic bile ducts arising from a ductal plate malformation
Caroli disease refers to isolated ductal ectasia, whereas Caroli syndrome denotes the same duct changes together with congenital hepatic fibrosis
It is part of the fibrocystic disease spectrum and is associated with renal cystic disease, including autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease and PKHD1 mutations
Bile stasis within the dilated ducts predisposes to intraductal stone formation, recurrent bacterial cholangitis, and abscess
The central dot sign on cross-sectional imaging, representing a portal vein branch surrounded by dilated duct, is a characteristic feature
There is an increased long-term risk of cholangiocarcinoma requiring vigilance
Management addresses cholangitis and stones, with segmental resection for localised disease and liver transplantation for diffuse or complicated disease
reference.pathophysiology: Caroli disease results from arrested remodelling of the embryonic ductal plate affecting the larger intrahepatic bile ducts, leaving them congenitally and permanently dilated in a saccular or fusiform pattern that communicates with the biliary tree. The abnormal ducts promote stasis of bile, which encourages the formation of pigment stones and repeated ascending bacterial infection, producing recurrent cholangitis and sometimes hepatic abscesses. When the same ductal plate malformation also involves the smallest ducts it produces the periportal fibrosis of congenital hepatic fibrosis, giving rise to Caroli syndrome with additional portal hypertension. The shared ciliopathy mechanism, often linked to PKHD1, accounts for the frequent association with renal cystic disease, and chronic biliary inflammation underlies the raised risk of cholangiocarcinoma.
additionalDifferentials: Obstructive biliary dilatation from stones or stricture
additionalInvestigations: Ultrasound and cross-sectional imaging showing intrahepatic ductal dilatation and the central dot sign
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography to map the biliary tree
Assessment for intraductal calculi and complications
Renal imaging and function tests for associated cystic kidney disease
Liver biopsy where congenital hepatic fibrosis is suspected (Caroli syndrome)
Tumour markers and targeted imaging when cholangiocarcinoma is a concern
redFlags: Fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain indicating acute cholangitis or sepsis
Progressive weight loss or a dominant stricture raising concern for cholangiocarcinoma
Features of portal hypertension when congenital hepatic fibrosis coexists
Recurrent severe infective episodes suggesting the need for definitive surgical management
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the extent of ductal involvement and the frequency of infective complications; localised disease may be cured by resection, whereas diffuse disease carries recurrent cholangitis, stone disease, and an elevated cholangiocarcinoma risk, with transplantation considered for advanced or complicated cases.
pitfalls: Confusing Caroli disease with primary sclerosing cholangitis or simple obstructive dilatation
Failing to distinguish isolated Caroli disease from Caroli syndrome with hepatic fibrosis and portal hypertension
Underestimating the long-term risk of cholangiocarcinoma and omitting surveillance
Delaying definitive surgical assessment in localised, recurrently infected disease
references: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Treat acute cholangitis promptly with appropriate antibiotics and biliary drainage
Clear intraductal calculi endoscopically or percutaneously and consider ursodeoxycholic acid to reduce stone formation and improve bile flow
Resect surgically where disease is localised to one lobe or segment, which can be curative
Manage portal hypertension and its complications in Caroli syndrome with congenital hepatic fibrosis
Maintain surveillance for cholangiocarcinoma, given the elevated long-term risk
Assess and manage associated renal cystic disease, including autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease
Refer for liver transplantation in diffuse or advanced disease with recurrent cholangitis
Offer genetic counselling for PKHD1-related fibrocystic disease and screen relatives where indicated
